summary: Describes the problem of rogue IPv6 Router Advertisements, where misconfigured or malicious devices announce themselves as routers and disrupt hosts that autoconfigure from those messages. It is a problem statement and is informational.

eli5.summary: In IPv6 a router announces itself to devices on a network. Sometimes a wrong device announces itself by mistake and everyone follows the wrong guide. This describes that problem.

questions: why are fake ipv6 router advertisements a problem
what is a rogue ipv6 router advertisement
how to stop rogue router advertisements
subtitle: Why stray IPv6 Router Advertisements break networks, and the menu of ways to stop them.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts take their default router and prefix straight from Router Advertisements (RAs), so an unintended RA from a misconfigured router or a user's laptop can cause partial or complete failure on a link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sorts the ways bogus RAs appear (administrator error, user error, malicious), then compares mitigations such as RA snooping, switch ACLs, SEND, Router Preference, host firewalls, deprecation daemons, Layer 2 partitioning and DHCPv6 options.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement, not a standard. It concludes that switch-based ACLs and RA-Guard-style approaches look simplest, with SEND a good longer-term answer.

today: RFC 6104 is an Informational problem statement, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RA-Guard approach it discusses is specified in RFC 6105.

sections.title: The Rogue RA Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 Router Advertisements (RAs), defined in Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861), carry the information a host uses to autoconfigure. The default router address is taken directly from the source address of the RA message, and the RA also tells hosts which prefixes to use for stateless address autoconfiguration (RFC 4862).

The authors observed undesired or bogus RAs on deployed networks, more often in shared wireless environments but also on wired enterprise networks. A bogus RA can cause partial or complete failure for hosts on the link. If good and bad RAs are mixed, a host might keep the good default gateway but pick a wrong source address, leading to egress filtering problems.

The document focuses on accidental rogue RAs, since these are the common case, and also covers how hosts can recover quickly from a wrong configuration.
sections.eli5: Devices on the network trust whoever shouts that they are the router. If the wrong device shouts, some devices follow it and their messages never arrive.

sections.title: Where Bogus RAs Come From
sections.content:
The RFC names three broad classes of scenario.

  • Administrator misconfiguration: a router interface is configured wrongly, so hosts build incorrect addresses or gateways, or a Layer 2 VLAN misconfiguration lets RAs flood onto unintended links.
  • User misconfiguration: a user's device sends RAs by accident. The typical case is a laptop with Windows Internet Connection Sharing (ICS) enabled, which can turn it into a 6to4 gateway and also start a rogue DHCPv4 server. Users also plug cables into the wrong sockets and bridge two subnets.
  • Malicious misconfiguration: an attacker sends RAs for denial of service or man-in-the-middle attacks. The authors note that reports of this are few, while accidental rogue RAs are very commonplace.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a grown-up sets up the router wrong, sometimes someone's laptop accidentally pretends to be a router, and rarely someone does it on purpose.

sections.title: Ways to Mitigate Rogue RAs
sections.content:
The RFC surveys ten approaches, each with drawbacks.

  • Manual configuration with RA processing disabled: resource intensive and error prone.
  • RA snooping in Layer 2 switches, like DHCP snooping, with RA-Guard (RFC 6105) as a candidate. It needs managed switches.
  • ACLs on managed switches that block RA ICMP messages on user ports.
  • SEND (RFC 3971): robust in principle, but at the time of writing few implementations existed and bootstrapping issues were raised.
  • Router Preference (RFC 4191): administrators use High and hope accidental RAs are Medium, which fails if a user also sets High.
  • Layer 2 admission control such as IEEE 802.1x: helps against attackers but not misconfiguration.
  • Host-based packet filters: pushes the problem into keeping filters correct.
  • A deprecation tool that sends an RA with router lifetime zero, such as KAME rafixd.
  • Layer 2 partitioning, which can increase address space consumption and cost.
  • DHCPv6 default gateway and prefix options, which shift the problem to rogue DHCPv6 servers.
sections.eli5: There are many ways to guard against fake announcements: write the answer down by hand, have the network switches block fakes, make routers prove who they are, or have a helper tell everyone to ignore the fake.

sections.title: Comparison and Related Issues
sections.content:
A matrix compares the mitigations for a rogue multicast RA caused by administrator or user error. The RFC adds that it does not consider how practical each measure is. On that basis RA snooping such as RA-Guard has merit, while manual configuration is less appealing, though RA-Guard was not yet fully defined or available.

Other issues the authors record: RAs can be sent unicast (Section 6.2.6 of RFC 4861), so a monitoring daemon might not see them; the rogue DHCP server threat model is similar but a rogue multicast RA can affect all hosts immediately, while a rogue DHCP server depends on lease timers; IPv4-only networks should care too, because hosts may start preferring IPv6 via a 6to4 host; monitoring tools should report RAs; hosts need to recover from bad state; and the offending source should ideally be isolated, for example with Network Access Control.

The conclusions say SEND is probably the most robust, but for many campus, conference and public networks simpler measures are needed. Switch ACLs and RA-Guard-style approaches are likely the simplest.
sections.eli5: None of the fixes is perfect. The easiest ones for most networks are to have the network switches ignore announcements coming from the wrong place.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document is about operational problems from unintended misconfiguration. Earlier drafts analysed malicious rogue RAs, but working group feedback was to focus on the accidental case, so attacks that combine rogue RAs with other attacks, such as malicious Neighbor Advertisements, are not addressed.

On the wire, malicious RAs generally look like accidental ones, though they are more likely to spoof the MAC or IPv6 source address of the genuine router or use a High Router Preference. The deprecation daemon could itself be used in a denial-of-service attack if it deprecated the genuine RA. Tools such as NDPMon may detect malicious activity.
sections.eli5: This guide is about mistakes, not attackers. Attackers are harder to stop because their fake announcements look just like real ones.
